title: Atomic UX Research: organize and understand your insights efficiently
description: How Daniel Pidcock's Atomic Research organizes research into reusable experiments, facts, insights and conclusions.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI agents that act inside the CRM and keep the person in control.

blocks.text: Have you ever found yourself lost in long research reports, trying to find that one crucial insight? Atomic Research is a way to make that simpler. Just like in Atomic Design, where small parts (atoms) are combined to build complete interfaces, Atomic Research proposes breaking research knowledge into smaller pieces that are easy to reuse.

Instead of writing lengthy reports, you break the data into “research atoms” and organize them to produce clear facts and insights. That makes learning continuous and keeps information always accessible, ideal for applying across different phases of the project.

blocks.caption: Instead of a report nobody rereads, small atoms of learning that anyone can find in seconds.

blocks.text: Imagine your team is redesigning the search feature of an e-commerce app. While running usability tests, you collect small insights instead of producing one heavy report. These small learnings, the “atoms,” are reused for quick, actionable analysis, creating a living, flexible knowledge base that's always ready to consult.
The model developed by Daniel Pidcock organizes the process into four stages:

blocks.caption: The model's four atoms, each answering one question.

items: Experiments (What did we do?): Tests, interviews or analyses that bring in the data. E.g.: Testing your app's new search bar.
Facts (What does this teach us?): Clear lessons drawn from the experiments. E.g.: 70% of users didn't understand the magnifying glass icon.
Insights (What does this make us think?): Hypotheses based on the facts. E.g.: Replacing the magnifying glass with a search field may improve the experience.
Conclusions (What will we do?): Decisions based on the insights. E.g.: Swap the icon for a text search field.

blocks.caption: Experiments generate facts, facts support insights and insights lead to decisions. The same fact can feed new insights later.

blocks.text: A practical example of Atomic Research
Say your team is developing a new page layout for an e-commerce site. During usability tests, you collect several “atoms” of information, such as:

items: Experiment: Users were asked to navigate to the checkout page.
Fact: 60% of users didn't notice the “Complete purchase” button right away.
Insight: The “Complete purchase” button isn't prominent enough.
Conclusion: Change the button's design to make it more visible and accessible.

blocks.text: These “atoms” can be organized, combined and reused in new experiments or design decisions, saving time and giving every stakeholder a clear view.
Tools like Miro, glean.ly, FigJam and Mural help implement Atomic Research. Visualize the whole research cycle, from experimentation to conclusion, with sticky notes organized in columns.

It makes insights easier to reuse, saving time and letting you apply learnings across different projects. For stakeholders, it's a quick, visual way to follow results and make decisions without wasting time on long reports.

blocks.caption: Small, reusable insights instead of forgotten reports.

blocks.text: Atomic Research changes the way UX Research data gets organized. Modular, agile and efficient, it makes the research process more dynamic, making sure valuable insights don't get lost and are applied whenever needed.
